sources.title: Chapter 3: Enhanced ER (EER) Model - Comprehensive Exam

questions.q: What is the primary difference between a database and a database management system (DBMS)?
o: A database is hardware, while a DBMS is software
A database is the data itself, while a DBMS is the software that manages the data
A database is for small datasets, while a DBMS is for large datasets
There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable
questions.e: A database is the collection of related data itself, while a DBMS is the software system that manages, accesses, modifies, and maintains that data. The DBMS provides the interface between users/applications and the database.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical advantage of using a DBMS over a file-based system?
questions.e: DBMS systems typically have HIGHER initial development costs compared to simple file-based systems due to software licensing, training, and setup. However, they provide controlled redundancy, data consistency, concurrent access, security, and recovery - benefits that file systems cannot easily provide.

questions.q: In which scenario would using a DBMS NOT be recommended?
o: A banking system requiring ACID compliance and multiple concurrent users
A simple embedded system with static data and severe hardware limitations
A university managing student records with frequent updates
An e-commerce platform handling thousands of transactions daily
questions.e: DBMS is not recommended for simple embedded systems with static data and severe hardware limitations. The overhead of a DBMS (memory, processing, storage) is unnecessary when data is static, there's no concurrent access, and hardware resources are constrained.

questions.q: What are "queries" and "transactions" in the context of database applications?
o: Queries are requests for data retrieval; transactions are collections of database operations
Queries modify data; transactions retrieve data
Both terms refer to the same concept
Queries are used by DBAs; transactions are used by end users
questions.e: Queries are requests that retrieve/read data from the database and generate results. Transactions are collections of database operations (reads and writes) that must be executed as a single logical unit to maintain database consistency.

questions.q: Which characteristic of the database approach allows a database to be "self-describing"?
o: The database stores the system catalog (metadata) along with the actual data
The database uses natural language processing
The database includes user manuals within its structure
questions.e: A database is "self-describing" because it stores not only the data itself but also a complete description of the database structure (metadata) in the system catalog. This includes table definitions, data types, constraints, and relationships - allowing the DBMS to work with different databases.

questions.q: What are the three levels of data abstraction in a database system?
o: Physical level, Logical level, View level
Input level, Processing level, Output level
User level, Application level, System level
Hardware level, Software level, Network level
questions.e: The three levels of data abstraction are: (1) Physical level - describes HOW data is actually stored, (2) Logical level - describes WHAT data is stored and relationships, (3) View level (External level) - shows different parts of the database to different users based on their needs.

questions.q: What is the difference between a database schema and a database instance?
o: Schema is the structure/design that rarely changes; instance is the actual data at a specific moment
Schema is the data; instance is the structure
Schema is for small databases; instance is for large databases
They are the same thing with different names
questions.e: A schema is the logical structure/design of the database that changes very infrequently (the blueprint). An instance is the actual data stored in the database at a particular moment in time, which changes frequently as data is inserted, updated, or deleted.

questions.q: Which schema describes the database design at the storage/physical level?
questions.e: The physical schema describes the database design at the physical/storage level how data is actually stored on disk, including file organization, storage structures, access paths, and indexes.

questions.q: What does the "A" in ACID stand for, and what does it guarantee?
o: Atomicity - ensures the "all or nothing" rule; transactions execute completely or not at all
Availability - ensures the database is always accessible
Accuracy - ensures all data is correct
Authentication - ensures only authorized users access data
questions.e: Atomicity ensures the "all or nothing" rule - a transaction is treated as a single unit that either executes completely or doesn't execute at all. If any part fails, the entire transaction is rolled back (aborted) and no partial changes are saved.

questions.q: What problem does the "Isolation" property solve in concurrent database systems?
o: It prevents transactions from interfering with each other when executing concurrently
It prevents data loss during system failures
It prevents unauthorized access to data
questions.e: Isolation prevents concurrent transactions from interfering with each other. It ensures that changes made by one transaction are not visible to other transactions until committed. This prevents problems like reading intermediate/inconsistent states when multiple transactions are executing simultaneously.

questions.q: If a bank transfer transaction fails after deducting money from Account A but before adding it to Account B, which ACID property was violated?
o: Atomicity - the transaction should have been all-or-nothing
Consistency - the total balance is no longer preserved
questions.e: Both Atomicity and Consistency were violated. Atomicity was violated because the transaction executed partially (not all-or-nothing). Consistency was violated because the total balance is no longer preserved - money was deducted but not added, breaking the integrity constraint that total money must remain constant.

questions.q: What does OLTP stand for and what is its significance in database systems?
o: Online Transaction Processing - handles hundreds of concurrent transactions per second
Offline Transaction Processing - handles batch transactions
Online Testing and Production - for quality assurance
Optimized Linear Transaction Protocol - for faster processing
questions.e: OLTP stands for Online Transaction Processing. It is a major part of database applications that allows hundreds or even thousands of concurrent transactions to execute per second in real-time. Examples include banking systems, reservation systems, and e-commerce platforms.

questions.q: What is the difference between "Casual End Users" and "Naive/Parametric-End-Users"?
o: Casual users access the database occasionally (e.g., managers); Naive users perform routine tasks with canned transactions (e.g., bank tellers)
Casual users are beginners; Naive users are experts
Casual users modify data; Naive users only read data
questions.e: Casual end users occasionally access the database and may need different queries each time typically middle or high level managers. Naive/Parametric end users make up a large portion of users whose main job involves constantly querying and updating the database using standard pre programmed queries (canned transactions) like bank tellers or reservation agents.

questions.q: What is the primary role of Database Designers?
o: Define the database content, structure, constraints, and communicate with end-users to understand their needs
Monitor database performance and authorize user access
Create the user interface for database applications
questions.e: Database Designers are responsible for defining the content, structure, constraints, and functions/transactions of the database. They must communicate with end users to understand their requirements and translate them into a database design that meets those needs.

questions.q: What are the three main sources of database security risks?
o: Malicious insider, Negligent person within organization, External attacker
Software bugs, Network issues, Power outages
User errors, System crashes, Data corruption
questions.e: The three main sources of database security risks are: (1) Malicious insider with ill-intent who has privileged access, (2) Negligent person within the organization who exposes the database through careless actions, (3) External attacker who obtains credentials through social engineering or other methods. Insider threats are the most common cause of security breaches.

questions.q: Which security component restricts database access ensuring only authorized users can view or modify data?
questions.e: Access Control restricts access to the database, ensuring only authorized users have permission to view or modify data. It involves user authentication, authorization, and role-based access controls to prevent unauthorized access.

questions.q: What is "metadata" in the context of database systems?
o: Data about data - the description and structure information stored in the system catalog
The actual data stored in database tables
questions.e: Metadata is "data about data" - it is the description and structural information about the database stored in the system catalog. This includes table definitions, column names and types, constraints, relationships, and other schema information rather than the actual data itself.

questions.q: A weak entity type always has a _______ participation constraint with respect to its identifying relationship.
questions.e: A weak entity type ALWAYS has total participation in its identifying relationship because it cannot exist without the owner entity. The weak entity is existence-dependent on its owner.

questions.q: The disjoint constraint in the EER model specifies that:
o: An entity can be a member of more than one subclass
An entity can be a member of only one subclass in a subclass relationship
All entities must belong to at least one subclass
Subclasses cannot have their own attributes
questions.e: The disjoint constraint specifies that an entity can be a member of AT MOST ONE subclass. This means subclasses are mutually exclusive. The symbol "d" in the circle represents disjoint.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes specialization in EER diagrams?
o: The process of combining several entity types into a higher-level entity type
The process of defining a set of subclasses of an entity type
The process of creating weak entities
questions.e: Specialization is a top-down design process where we define a set of subclasses of an entity type. We start with an entity type and define specialized subclasses based on distinguishing characteristics.

questions.q: What symbol is used in EER diagrams to represent the subset (IS-A) relationship?
o: A circle with a 'd' inside for disjoint
questions.e: A circle with "d" inside represents disjoint subclasses, while a circle with "o"-represents-overlapping.-The-circle-itself-represents-the-IS-A-(subset)-relationship-in-specialization/generalization-hierarchies.

questions.q: In a total specialization constraint:
o: Every entity in the superclass must belong to at least one subclass
Some entities in the superclass may not belong to any subclass
Entities can belong to multiple subclasses
The superclass cannot have its own attributes
questions.e: Total specialization (shown by a double line) means every entity in the superclass MUST belong to at least one subclass. Partial specialization allows entities to not belong to any subclass.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about generalization is TRUE?
o: It is a bottom-up design process
It is a top-down design process
It always results in disjoint subclasses
It cannot be used with weak entities
questions.e: Generalization is a bottom-up design process where we combine several entity types with common features into a higher-level generic entity type (superclass). Specialization is top-down.

questions.q: A union type (category) in EER diagrams:
o: Represents a single superclass with multiple subclasses
Represents a subclass with multiple superclasses
questions.e: A union type (category) represents a subclass that has multiple superclasses. It is denoted by the symbol ∪ and models the union of different entity types.

questions.q: What is the difference between overlapping and disjoint constraints?
o: Overlapping allows an entity to belong to multiple subclasses; disjoint does not
Disjoint allows an entity to belong to multiple subclasses; overlapping does not
They are the same concept with different names
Overlapping is used for weak entities only
questions.e: Overlapping constraint (represented by "o") allows an entity to be a member of multiple subclasses simultaneously. Disjoint constraint (represented by "d") requires membership in at most one subclass.

questions.q: In an EER diagram, a subclass discriminator attribute:
o: Determines which subclass an entity belongs to
Is always required for all specializations
Cannot be used with overlapping constraints
questions.e: A subclass discriminator is an attribute of the superclass that determines subclass membership. For example, "employee_type" might determine if an employee is a secretary, engineer, or technician.

questions.q: Which of the following is TRUE about attribute inheritance in EER?
o: Subclasses inherit all attributes from their superclass
Inheritance only applies to key attributes
questions.e: Subclasses inherit ALL attributes and relationships from their superclass(es). This is a fundamental principle of specialization/generalization hierarchies. Subclasses can also have their own specific attributes.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about shared subclasses is TRUE? (Select all that apply)
o: A shared subclass can have multiple superclasses
A shared subclass inherits attributes from all its superclasses
Shared subclasses are also called multiple inheritance
Shared subclasses can only exist in overlapping specializations
questions.e: A shared subclass (multiple inheritance) has multiple superclasses and inherits attributes from all of them. This is also called multiple inheritance. Option d is incorrect because shared subclasses can exist in both overlapping and disjoint specializations.

questions.q: In EER diagrams, what does a double-lined rectangle represent?
questions.e: A double-lined rectangle represents a weak entity type. The double lines indicate that the entity is existence-dependent on another entity and cannot be uniquely identified by its own attributes alone.

questions.q: Which notation is used to show total specialization in an EER diagram?
o: A single line from superclass to the specialization circle
A double line from superclass to the specialization circle
A dashed line from superclass to the specialization circle
questions.e: Total specialization is shown by a double line from the superclass to the specialization circle. This indicates that every entity in the superclass must belong to at least one subclass. A single line indicates partial specialization.

questions.q: Derived attributes in EER diagrams are shown using:
questions.e: Derived attributes are shown using a dashed line oval in ER/EER diagrams. Derived attributes are those whose values can be calculated from other attributes (e.g., age can be derived from date_of_birth).

questions.q: What does EER stand for and what does it add to the basic ER model?
o: Enhanced Entity-Relationship; adds subclasses/superclasses, specialization/generalization, and categories
Extended Entity-Relationship; adds only subclasses and superclasses
Enhanced Entity-Relationship; adds only specialization hierarchies
Extended Entity-Relationship; adds foreign key constraints
questions.e: EER stands for Enhanced Entity Relationship (also called Extended ER). It extends the basic ER model by adding three additional concepts: subclasses/superclasses, specialization/generalization hierarchies, and categories (UNION types). These additions enable modeling of more complex database applications.

questions.q: Why do we need subclasses in database modeling?
o: To represent meaningful subgroupings of entities with specific attributes and relationships
To reduce the size of the database
questions.e: Subclasses are needed to represent meaningful subgroupings of entities that have specific attributes and relationships that don't apply to all entities in the superclass. This allows more precise modeling of real-world scenarios where entities have both common and specific characteristics.

questions.q: In the EMPLOYEE example, SECRETARY, ENGINEER, and TECHNICIAN are subclasses. What is the basis for this grouping?
o: Job type - the employee's specific job role
questions.e: SECRETARY, ENGINEER, and TECHNICIAN are subclasses based on Job Type - the specific job role of the employee. This is an attribute-defined specialization where Job_type is the defining attribute (discriminator) that determines which subclass an employee belongs to.

questions.q: What are "subtypes" in EER modeling?
o: Another term for subclasses - meaningful subgroupings of a superclass entity type
questions.e: Subtypes are another term for subclasses - they represent meaningful subgroupings of entities from a superclass entity type. The terms "subclass" and "subtype" are used interchangeably in EER modeling.

questions.q: A subclass entity is a member of which entity types?
o: Both the subclass AND its superclass
questions.e: A subclass entity is a member of BOTH the subclass AND its superclass. This is fundamental to inheritance - the entity has all characteristics of both the general superclass and the specific subclass.

questions.q: What is specialization in EER modeling?
o: The process of defining a set of subclasses of an entity type (top-down approach)
The process of combining multiple entity types into one (bottom-up approach)
The process of creating relationships between entities
The process of normalizing a database
questions.e: Specialization is the process of defining a set of subclasses of an entity type. It is a top-down approach where you start with a general entity type and identify meaningful specialized subgroupings. For example, starting with EMPLOYEE and specializing into SECRETARY, ENGINEER, TECHNICIAN.

questions.q: What is an "attribute-defined specialization" or "discriminator"?
o: A specialization where all subclasses have membership condition based on the same superclass attribute
A specialization based on relationship types
A specialization that doesn't use attributes
A specialization that merges multiple superclasses
questions.e: An attribute-defined specialization occurs when all subclasses have their membership condition based on the same attribute of the superclass. This attribute is called the defining attribute or discriminator. For example, Job_type determines whether an EMPLOYEE is a SECRETARY, ENGINEER, or TECHNICIAN.

questions.q: In the EMPLOYEE example with SECRETARY, TECHNICIAN, and ENGINEER subclasses, what is the defining attribute (discriminator)?
questions.e: Job_type is the defining attribute (discriminator) that determines which subclass an employee belongs to. The value of Job_type (e.g., "Secretary", "Engineer", "Technician") determines the employee's membership in the corresponding subclass.

questions.q: What is a specialization hierarchy?
o: A structure where every subclass has at most one superclass (single inheritance)
A structure where subclasses can have multiple superclasses
questions.e: A specialization hierarchy is a structure where every subclass participates as a subclass in only one superclass relationship. This means each subclass has at most one superclass, creating a single inheritance hierarchy (tree structure).

questions.q: What are the two main types of constraints that apply to specialization and generalization?
o: Primary key constraint and Foreign key constraint
questions.e: The two basic constraints are: (1) Disjointness Constraint - determines whether subclasses must be disjoint or can overlap, and (2) Completeness (Exhaustiveness) Constraint - determines whether every superclass entity must belong to a subclass (total) or not (partial).

questions.q: What is an "overlapping" specialization?
o: A specialization where an entity can be a member of more than one subclass; represented by 'o' in EER diagrams
A specialization where subclasses must be disjoint; represented by 'd'
questions.e: An overlapping specialization (represented by "o" in EER diagrams) allows the same entity to be a member of more than one subclass. This is the opposite of disjoint. For example, an EMPLOYEE could be both a MANAGER and an ENGINEER simultaneously.

questions.q: How is a "total" specialization represented in an EER diagram?
o: A double line connecting the superclass to the circle
A single line connecting the superclass to the circle
questions.e: A total specialization is represented by a double line connecting the superclass to the circle in the EER diagram. This indicates that every entity in the superclass must participate in at least one subclass - similar to total participation constraint in ER diagrams.

questions.q: What happens when you delete an entity from a superclass?
o: It is automatically deleted from all subclasses to which it belongs
Only the superclass data is deleted
questions.e: When you delete an entity from a superclass, it is automatically deleted from all subclasses to which it belongs. This maintains referential integrity - a subclass entity cannot exist without its corresponding superclass entity.

questions.q: When inserting an entity in a superclass of a TOTAL specialization, what must happen?
o: The entity must be inserted in at least one of the subclasses
The entity cannot be inserted in any subclass
The entity must be inserted in all subclasses
questions.e: In a total specialization, when you insert an entity into the superclass, it MUST be inserted into at least one of the subclasses. This enforces the total completeness constraint - every superclass entity must participate in the specialization.

questions.q: In an EER diagram, what does the symbol 'd' inside a circle represent?
o: Disjoint constraint - subclasses are disjoint (entity can be in at most one subclass)
questions.e: The symbol "d" inside a circle represents the disjoint constraint in an EER diagram. It specifies that the subclasses must be disjoint - an entity can be a member of at most one subclass in the specialization.

questions.q: What is a "category" or "UNION type" in EER modeling?
o: A subclass that has several possible superclasses representing different entity types; a subset of the UNION of distinct entity types
questions.e: A category (UNION type) is a subclass that has several possible superclasses representing different entity types. It represents a collection of entities that is a subset of the UNION of distinct entity types. Unlike regular specialization where subclasses share the same superclass, categories allow multiple different superclasses.

questions.q: Can the superclasses of a category have different key attributes?
o: Yes, superclasses may have different key attributes or the same key attribute
No, they must always have the same key
No, they cannot have any keys
Only if they are weak entities
questions.e: Yes, the superclasses of a category may have different key attributes (as in OWNER category with PERSON, BANK, COMPANY) or they may have the same key attribute (as in REGISTERED_VEHICLE). This flexibility is one feature that distinguishes categories from regular specialization.

questions.q: How is a total category represented in an EER diagram?
o: A double line connecting the category and the circle
A single line connecting the category and the circle
questions.e: A total category is represented by a double line connecting the category and the circle in the EER diagram. This indicates that the category includes the complete union of all entities from its superclasses.

questions.q: What are the three main EER concepts that improve the expressive power of ER diagrams?
o: Primary keys, Foreign keys, and Constraints
questions.e: The three main EER concepts that improve expressive power are: (1) Superclasses and subclasses with specialization/generalization, (2) Categories or UNION types, and (3) Aggregation. These enable modeling of very complex database applications beyond what basic ER can handle.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly defines a relation in the relational model?
o: A collection of unrelated data stored in files
A two-dimensional table consisting of rows (tuples) and columns (attributes) with atomic values
A set of procedures for managing database files
A connection between two database tables
questions.e: A relation is formally defined as a two-dimensional table where each row represents a tuple (entity instance) and each column represents an attribute. All values in cells must be atomic (indivisible, single-valued).

questions.q: What is the degree (or arity) of a relation?
o: The number of tuples in the relation
The number of attributes (columns) in the relation
The total number of cells in the relation
questions.e: The degree (or arity) of a relation refers to the number of columns/attributes. For example, a relation with 5 attributes has a degree of 5. The number of tuples (rows) is called the cardinality.

questions.q: In the relational model, what is cardinality?
o: The number of attributes in a relation
The number of tuples (rows) in a relation at a particular moment
The degree of dependency between two relations
The maximum number of relationships between entities
questions.e: Cardinality refers to the number of tuples (rows) currently in a relation. It changes whenever data is inserted, deleted, or updated. Degree refers to the number of attributes. Cardinality is dynamic; degree is static.

questions.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of the relational model?
o: Allows composite and multivalued attributes within a single relation
All values in a tuple must be atomic (indivisible)
Tuples within a relation are ordered by default
Attributes can have NULL values without restriction
questions.e: The First Normal Form (1NF) constraint requires that all values in a relation must be atomic. This means no composite or multivalued attributes are allowed within a single cell. Each cell contains exactly one value.

questions.q: What is a superkey?
o: A single attribute that uniquely identifies a tuple
A set of one or more attributes that uniquely identifies a tuple
The primary key of a relation
A foreign key that references another relation
questions.e: A superkey is a set of attributes (one or more) that can uniquely identify a tuple in a relation. A key is a minimal superkey (removing any attribute makes it non-unique). Every key is a superkey, but not every superkey is a key.

questions.q: What is the difference between a key and a superkey?
o: There is no difference; they are the same thing
A key is a minimal superkey; removing any attribute from a key makes it non-unique
A superkey is always smaller than a key
A key can have NULL values, but a superkey cannot
questions.e: A key is a MINIMAL superkey. This means: (1) It uniquely identifies each tuple, and (2) Removing any attribute from it would destroy the uniqueness property. A superkey doesn't have to be minimal.

questions.q: Which constraint ensures that no primary key attribute can have a NULL value?
questions.e: Entity Integrity Constraint states that the primary key attributes of a relation cannot be NULL. This ensures that every tuple can be uniquely identified and distinguished from others.

questions.q: What is the primary function of a foreign key?
o: To uniquely identify a tuple within its own relation
To link tuples from one relation to tuples in another relation
To enforce domain constraints on attributes
To prevent duplicate values in a column
questions.e: A foreign key is an attribute (or set of attributes) in one relation that references the primary key of another relation. It maintains relationships between tables and enforces referential integrity.

questions.q: Which statement is true regarding Referential Integrity?
o: Every primary-key value must match a primary-key value in an associated table
Every primary-key value must match a foreign-key value in an associated table
Every foreign-key value must match a foreign-key value in an associated table
Every foreign-key value must match a primary-key value in an associated table
questions.e: Referential Integrity states that every value of a foreign key must either: (1) Match an existing primary key value in the referenced relation, or (2) Be NULL. This prevents orphaned records.

questions.q: What does the domain constraint specify in the relational model?
o: That each attribute value must come from the specified data type domain
That primary keys must be unique
That no two tuples can have the same values
questions.e: Domain constraints specify that each attribute value must be atomic and come from the specified domain (data type). For example, if an attribute is defined as INTEGER, only integer values are allowed.

questions.q: Entity Integrity constraint ensures that no primary key attribute can be null.
questions.e: TRUE. The Entity Integrity constraint requires all primary key attributes to have non-NULL values to ensure each tuple is uniquely identifiable.

questions.q: In the relational model, the order of tuples in a relation is significant.
questions.e: FALSE. The relational model treats a relation as a SET of tuples, not a sequence. Row order is not meaningful. The only order that matters is the order of attribute definitions in the schema.

questions.q: A relation can have multiple primary keys.
questions.e: FALSE. Each relation has exactly ONE primary key. However, a relation can have multiple CANDIDATE KEYS. One candidate key is chosen as the primary key; the others are called alternate keys.

questions.q: The degree of a relation can change dynamically as new records are inserted.
questions.e: FALSE. The degree (number of attributes) is fixed in the schema. Only cardinality (number of tuples) changes dynamically.

questions.q: Define what a relation schema is and explain the difference between a relation schema and a relation instance.
questions.m: A-relation-schema-is-the-logical-description/definition-of-a-relation,-consisting-of: -Relation-name -Attribute-names-and-their-data-types A-relation-instance-is-the-actual-data-(tuples/rows)-in-the-relation-at-a-particular-moment. Key-differences: -Schema:-Static-(rarely-changes),-defines-structure -Instance:-Dynamic-(changes-with-INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE),-contains-actual-data
questions.e: Schema defines WHAT data can be stored; instance shows WHAT data IS currently stored.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a KEY and a SUPERKEY with an example.
questions.m: KEY: A minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies tuples. Removing ANY attribute destroys uniqueness. SUPERKEY: Any set of attributes that uniquely identifies tuples, but may contain extra attributes. Example with Student relation: Candidate KEYS: {ID}, {Email} SUPERKEYS: {ID}, {Email}, {ID, Email}, {ID, Email, Name} Every key IS a superkey, but not every superkey IS a key.
questions.e: Choose keys over superkeys for efficiency - smaller attribute sets mean faster lookups.

questions.q: List and explain at least 4 characteristics that define a relation in the relational model.
questions.m: 1. ATOMIC VALUES: All values must be indivisible (First Normal Form) 2. NO DUPLICATE TUPLES: Each tuple is unique 3. UNORDERED TUPLES: Tuples are treated as a SET, not a sequence 4. UNORDERED ATTRIBUTES: Column order is not significant 5. DOMAIN CONSTRAINT: Each attribute has a defined data type 6. TUPLE UNIQUENESS: Every tuple is uniquely identifiable via primary key
questions.e: These characteristics form the foundation of the relational model.

questions.q: Explain Entity Integrity and Referential Integrity constraints and their importance.
questions.m: ENTITY INTEGRITY: - Primary key attributes cannot be NULL - Ensures each tuple is uniquely identifiable REFERENTIAL INTEGRITY: - Foreign key values must match existing primary key values or be NULL - Prevents orphaned records IMPORTANCE: - Entity Integrity: Guarantees tuple identity - Referential Integrity: Maintains consistency between tables
questions.e: These constraints prevent invalid and inconsistent data.

questions.q: Given the CAR relation: CAR(State, Reg#, SerialNo, Make, Model, Year) Data: | State | Reg# | SerialNo | Make | Model | | TX | 1234 | ABC123 | Ford | Focus | | CA | 5678 | XYZ789 | Honda | Civic | Identify: (a) All candidate keys, (b) List 3 superkeys, (c) Choose and justify a primary key.
questions.m: (a) CANDIDATE KEYS: - {State, Reg#} - {SerialNo} (b) SUPERKEYS: 1. {SerialNo} 2. {State, Reg#} 3. {State, Reg#, SerialNo} 4. {SerialNo, Make} (c) PRIMARY KEY: {SerialNo} Justification: Single attribute, smaller than {State, Reg#}, faster lookups, globally unique like VIN.
questions.e: Choose the smallest candidate key for efficiency.

questions.q: What does the SELECT statement do in SQL?
o: Creates a new table in the database
Retrieves data from one or more tables
Modifies existing data in a table
questions.e: The SELECT statement is used to retrieve (query) data from a database. It allows you to specify which columns and rows you want to fetch from one or more tables.

questions.q: In SQL, which keyword removes duplicate rows from query results?
questions.e: The DISTINCT keyword eliminates duplicate tuples from the result set. By default, SELECT returns all rows including duplicates (SELECT ALL is implicit).

questions.q: Which SQL clause is used to filter rows based on conditions?
questions.e: The WHERE clause specifies conditions that rows must satisfy to be included in the result set. It performs selection (restriction) of tuples based on predicates.

questions.q: What is the correct syntax for a basic SELECT statement?
questions.e: The correct syntax is: SELECT [columns] FROM [table] WHERE [condition]. The FROM clause specifies the table(s), WHERE filters rows, and SELECT specifies which columns to return.

questions.q: Which of the following SQL statements would retrieve all employees with a salary greater than 50000?
questions.e: The > operator is used for "greater than".-The-WHERE-clause-is-for-filtering-rows.-HAVING-is-used-after-GROUP-BY-for-aggregate-conditions.

questions.q: Which SQL command is used to insert new rows into a table?
questions.e: The INSERT statement adds new records/tuples to a table. Syntax: INSERT INTO table VALUES (...) or INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (...).

questions.q: What does the UPDATE statement do?
o: Modifies existing data in a table
Adds new rows to a table
questions.e: The UPDATE statement modifies existing data in one or more columns of existing rows. Syntax: UPDATE table SET column=value WHERE condition;

questions.q: Which SQL statement removes all rows from a table permanently?
questions.e: DELETE FROM removes rows. DROP TABLE removes the entire table. TRUNCATE removes all data but is faster. DELETE is more commonly used for removing specific or all rows.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the ORDER BY clause?
o: Sort the result set by one or more columns
questions.e: ORDER BY sorts the result set in ascending (ASC) or descending (DESC) order based on specified column(s). Default is ascending.

questions.q: In SQL, what is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column_name)?
o: They are identical and can be used interchangeably
COUNT(*) counts all rows including NULL values; COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values in that column
questions.e: COUNT(*) counts all rows in a result set, including those with NULL values. COUNT(column) counts only non-NULL values in that specific column.

questions.q: In SQL, the WHERE clause can use aggregate functions like COUNT() or SUM().
questions.e: FALSE. The WHERE clause filters individual rows before aggregation. Aggregate conditions are applied AFTER grouping using the HAVING clause, not WHERE.

questions.q: SQL is a declarative language, meaning you specify WHAT you want, not HOW to get it.
questions.e: TRUE. SQL is declarative - you state the desired result without specifying the algorithm to retrieve it. The DBMS determines the execution plan.

questions.q: The ORDER BY clause must appear before the WHERE clause in a SELECT statement.
questions.e: FALSE. The correct order is: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... ORDER BY. WHERE comes before ORDER BY in SQL syntax.

questions.q: A JOIN operation in SQL combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column.
questions.e: TRUE. JOINs combine data from multiple tables using a join condition (usually matching primary and foreign keys).

questions.q: Explain the difference between the DELETE statement and the TRUNCATE statement. When would you use each?
questions.m: DELETE: - Removes rows one by one - Can use WHERE clause for conditional deletion - Slower for large datasets - Can be rolled back (if in transaction) - Logs each deleted row TRUNCATE: - Removes all rows at once - Cannot use WHERE clause - Much faster - Uses minimal transaction log space - Resets identity seed (if auto-increment) Use DELETE when you need to delete specific rows or preserve identity values. Use TRUNCATE when you need to empty an entire table quickly.
questions.e: Both remove data but work differently - DELETE is row-by-row and flexible; TRUNCATE is bulk and fast.

questions.q: What is the difference between INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, and RIGHT JOIN? Provide a brief explanation of when to use each.
questions.m: INNER JOIN: - Returns only rows where there is a match in BOTH tables - Excludes unmatched rows - Use when you need only matching records LEFT JOIN (LEFT OUTER JOIN): - Returns ALL rows from left table - Includes matching rows from right table - Unmatched right rows shown as NULL - Use when you want all records from the left table RIGHT JOIN (RIGHT OUTER JOIN): - Returns ALL rows from right table - Includes matching rows from left table - Unmatched left rows shown as NULL - Use when you want all records from the right table Example: LEFT JOIN keeps all employees even if not assigned to projects.
questions.e: JOINs determine which rows are preserved when combining tables.

questions.q: Explain what the GROUP BY clause does and why it is used with aggregate functions.
questions.m: GROUP BY groups rows with identical values in specified column(s). Purpose: - Divide data into meaningful categories - Apply aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN) to each group - Generate summary reports Example: GROUP BY department calculates total salary per department. Key points: - Non-grouped columns in SELECT must use aggregate functions - Filters applied after grouping use HAVING (not WHERE) - NULL values form their own group
questions.e: GROUP BY enables aggregate analysis at category level rather than row level.

questions.q: Write a SQL query for this requirement: From the EMPLOYEE table, retrieve the employee ID, name, and salary for all employees in the IT department with salary greater than 60000. Order the results by salary in descending order.
questions.m: SELECT EmployeeID, Name, Salary FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Department = 'IT' AND Salary > 60000 ORDER BY Salary DESC;
questions.e: The query uses SELECT for columns, FROM for the table, WHERE for filtering conditions (both department and salary), and ORDER BY DESC for descending salary order.

questions.q: Write a SQL query to find the total number of employees in each department, showing department name and employee count. Only include departments with more than 5 employees.
questions.m: SELECT d.DepartmentName, COUNT(e.EmployeeID) AS EmployeeCount FROM DEPARTMENT d LEFT JOIN EMPLOYEE e ON d.DepartmentID = e.DepartmentID GROUP BY d.DepartmentName HAVING COUNT(e.EmployeeID) > 5;
questions.e: Uses COUNT(*) with GROUP BY for aggregation, HAVING for filtering groups, and JOIN to connect department and employee tables.

questions.q: Write a SQL query to retrieve all customers who placed at least one order with a total amount exceeding $500.
questions.m: SELECT DISTINCT c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName FROM CUSTOMER c JOIN ORDER o ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID WHERE o.OrderAmount > 500;
questions.e: Uses DISTINCT to avoid duplicates when a customer has multiple qualifying orders. WHERE filters by order amount. JOIN connects customer and order tables.

questions.q: What does a NULL value represent in SQL?
questions.e: NULL represents data that is unknown, missing, unavailable, or not applicable. It is NOT the same as zero, empty string, or false. NULL comparisons use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.

questions.q: In SQL, how do you compare values with NULL?
questions.e: Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to check for NULL values. The = and <> operators don't work with NULL because NULL comparisons always return unknown, not true or false.

questions.q: Which aggregate function returns the highest value in a column?
questions.e: The MAX() function returns the maximum/highest value. Similarly, MIN() returns the minimum/lowest value in a column.

questions.q: What does the LIKE operator do in SQL?
o: Checks if two values are equal
Performs pattern matching in text searches
questions.e: LIKE is used for pattern matching. It uses wildcards: % (zero or more characters) and _ (single character). Example: WHERE name LIKE 'A%' finds names starting with A.

questions.q: Which of the following SQL queries will return sailors who have reserved boat number 103?
o: SELECT sname FROM Sailors WHERE sid = 103;
SELECT S.sname FROM Sailors S, Reserves R WHERE S.sid = R.sid AND R.bid = 103;
SELECT sname FROM Sailors WHERE bid = 103;
questions.e: Option B correctly joins Sailors and Reserves tables on sid and filters for bid = 103. This returns sailor names who have reserved boat 103. Option A checks sid = 103 (wrong attribute), C tries to use bid in Sailors table (doesn't exist), and D returns reservation records, not sailor names.

questions.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING clauses in SQL?
o: WHERE filters tuples before grouping, HAVING filters groups after grouping
WHERE and HAVING are exactly the same
WHERE is used with aggregates, HAVING is not
HAVING can only be used with COUNT function
questions.e: WHERE filters individual tuples BEFORE grouping occurs, while HAVING filters groups AFTER grouping. WHERE cannot use aggregate functions directly, but HAVING can. For example: WHERE Salary > 30000 filters employees first, then GROUP BY groups them, then HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 filters the groups.

questions.q: Which SQL query returns the name and age of the youngest sailor?
o: SELECT sname, age FROM Sailors WHERE age = MIN(age);
SELECT sname, age FROM Sailors WHERE age <= ALL(SELECT age FROM Sailors);
SELECT sname, age FROM Sailors ORDER BY age LIMIT 1;
questions.e: Option B uses ALL to compare with all ages in the subquery, correctly finding the youngest. Option A won't work because you can't use aggregate in WHERE without subquery. Option C returns only the age, not name. Option D works in MySQL but isn't standard SQL and doesn't handle ties.

questions.q: What is the result of a LEFT OUTER JOIN?
o: Returns only matching tuples from both tables
Returns all tuples from the left table, with NULLs for non-matching right table tuples
Returns all tuples from the right table only
Returns the Cartesian product of both tables
questions.e: LEFT OUTER JOIN returns ALL tuples from the left table. If a left tuple has no match in the right table, NULL values are filled in for right table attributes. INNER JOIN (A) only returns matches. RIGHT OUTER JOIN (C) keeps all right tuples. CROSS JOIN (D) is Cartesian product.

questions.q: Which aggregate function should be used to count unique values in a column?
questions.e: COUNT(DISTINCT column_name) counts only unique/distinct values in a column. COUNT(*) counts all rows including duplicates. SUM(DISTINCT) adds unique values (rarely used). UNIQUE() is not a standard SQL function.

questions.q: What does the EXISTS operator do in a nested query?
o: Returns TRUE if the subquery returns at least one tuple
Returns TRUE only if the subquery returns exactly one tuple
Counts the number of tuples in the subquery
Checks if a value exists in a list
questions.e: EXISTS returns TRUE if the subquery result contains at least one tuple, FALSE otherwise. It's used for checking existence, not counting. NOT EXISTS checks for non-existence. EXISTS is often more efficient than IN for large datasets because it stops as soon as it finds one match.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a VIEW in SQL?
o: To create a virtual table based on a query that doesn't store data physically
To delete tables from the database
questions.e: A VIEW is a virtual table defined by a query. It doesn't physically store data (unless materialized). Views are useful for: security (hiding sensitive columns), simplifying complex queries, providing different user perspectives, and abstracting the database structure.

questions.q: Which of the following is a correlated nested query?
o: SELECT * FROM Employee WHERE Dno IN (SELECT Dnumber FROM Department);
SELECT * FROM Employee E WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee WHERE Dno = E.Dno);
questions.e: Option B is correlated because the subquery references the outer query (E.Dno). The subquery must be executed for each tuple in the outer query. Non-correlated queries (A, C, D) execute the subquery once and use the result in the outer query.

questions.q: What is NULL in SQL?
o: A special value representing unknown, unavailable, or not applicable data
questions.e: NULL represents unknown, unavailable, or not applicable data. It's NOT zero (numeric), empty string (text), or false (boolean). NULL has special comparison rules: NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN (not TRUE). Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to check for NULL values.

questions.q: Which operator is used to check if a value is NULL?
questions.e: IS NULL is the correct operator to check for NULL values. = NULL doesn't work because NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN in SQL's three-valued logic. Use: WHERE column IS NULL or WHERE column IS NOT NULL.

questions.q: What is the primary goal of normalization in database design?
o: To increase the size of the database
To minimize redundancy and improve data consistency
To increase the number of tables
questions.e: Normalization aims to reduce redundancy, eliminate anomalies, and improve data integrity. It minimizes duplicate data storage and ensures consistency.

questions.q: What is a functional dependency in the context of normalization?
o: When the value of one attribute determines the value of another attribute
A constraint that enforces primary keys
The order in which attributes appear in a table
questions.e: A functional dependency (X → Y) means if two tuples have the same X value, they must have the same Y value. It is a relationship between attributes within a table.

questions.q: Which normal form eliminates repeating groups?
questions.e: First Normal Form (1NF) requires all attribute values to be atomic (no composite or multivalued attributes). This eliminates repeating groups and ensures atomicity.

questions.q: What is a partial dependency?
o: A dependency on part of a composite primary key
A functional dependency on a foreign key
A dependency that cannot be removed
questions.e: A partial dependency occurs when a non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite primary key, not the entire key. This violates 2NF.

questions.q: A relation is in Second Normal Form (2NF) if:
o: It is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute is fully dependent on the entire primary key
It is in 1NF and has no transitive dependencies
It has only one candidate key
questions.e: 2NF requires: (1) The relation is in 1NF, and (2) Every non-prime attribute is FULLY functionally dependent on the primary key (not just part of it).

questions.q: What is a transitive dependency?
o: A dependency where X → Y and Y → Z, so X → Z
A dependency between two foreign keys
A dependency on the order of attributes
A dependency that increases with more data
questions.e: A transitive dependency occurs when: X → Y and Y → Z (where Y is not a candidate key), then X → Z. This violates 3NF.

questions.q: A relation is in Third Normal Form (3NF) if:
o: It is in 2NF and has no transitive dependencies on the primary key
Every attribute is a primary key
questions.e: 3NF requires: (1) The relation is in 2NF, and (2) No non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on the primary key.

questions.q: What is BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form)?
o: A form where every determinant is a candidate key
A form that eliminates all foreign keys
questions.e: BCNF is stricter than 3NF. It requires that every determinant (attribute on which another depends) must be a candidate key. Every BCNF relation is in 3NF, but not vice versa.

questions.q: What is an insertion anomaly?
o: Unable to insert data due to a primary key constraint
Unable to insert a new record because required attributes are missing
questions.e: An insertion anomaly occurs when you cannot insert data without inserting unrelated data. Example: Cannot add a new course unless you assign it to a student.

questions.q: What is a deletion anomaly?
o: Deleting a record you did not intend to delete
Losing valid data when deleting unrelated data
questions.e: A deletion anomaly occurs when deleting data results in unintended loss of other information. Example: Deleting the only employee in a department deletes the department data too.

questions.q: What is an update anomaly?
o: Having to update the same information in multiple places for consistency
questions.e: An update anomaly occurs when you must update the same fact in multiple rows to maintain consistency. This is caused by redundancy and violates normalization principles.

questions.q: Every relation in BCNF is also in 3NF.
questions.e: TRUE. BCNF is a stricter form of 3NF. Every BCNF relation must be in 3NF, though not every 3NF relation is in BCNF.

questions.q: A functional dependency X → Y means X is a primary key.
questions.e: FALSE. A functional dependency X → Y means X determines Y, but X does not have to be a primary key. Any attribute(s) can have functional dependencies.

questions.q: Normalization always improves query performance.
questions.e: FALSE. While normalization improves data integrity and reduces redundancy, it may require more JOINs in queries, potentially slowing retrieval. Sometimes denormalization is chosen for performance.

questions.q: A relation with all atomic values is automatically in First Normal Form.
questions.e: TRUE. 1NF requires all values to be atomic (indivisible). This is the fundamental requirement and is the starting point for further normalization.

questions.q: Explain the difference between 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF. What problem does each form address?
questions.m: 1NF (First Normal Form): - Problem: Repeating groups and non-atomic values - Solution: All values must be atomic (indivisible) - No composite or multivalued attributes in cells 2NF (Second Normal Form): - Problem: Partial dependencies - Solution: Every non-prime attribute must be FULLY dependent on the entire primary key - No non-key attribute depends on just part of a composite key 3NF (Third Normal Form): - Problem: Transitive dependencies - Solution: No non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on the primary key - If X → Y and Y → Z (Y not a key), then Y and Z are in another relation Progression: 1NF addresses atomicity → 2NF addresses key dependencies → 3NF addresses non-key dependencies
questions.e: Each normal form builds on the previous one, eliminating specific types of anomalies.

questions.q: Define functional dependency and provide two examples with actual attributes.
questions.m: A functional dependency is a relationship between attributes where one attribute (or group) determines another. Definition: X → Y means if two tuples have the same X value, they must have the same Y value. Example 1: SSN → EmployeeName - If two records have the same SSN, they must have the same employee name - SSN uniquely identifies an employee Example 2: CourseID → CourseName - If two records have the same CourseID, they must have the same course name - CourseID uniquely identifies a course Example 3: (StudentID, CourseID) → Grade - The combination of StudentID and CourseID determines the grade - A specific student in a specific course has one grade
questions.e: Functional dependencies are the foundation of normalization and must be identified before decomposing relations.

questions.q: Explain the differences between insertion, deletion, and update anomalies with concrete examples.
questions.m: UPDATE ANOMALY: - Problem: Changing one fact requires updating multiple rows - Example: If student name appears in 5 different records, changing their name requires 5 updates - Risk: If you miss one update, data becomes inconsistent INSERTION ANOMALY: - Problem: Cannot insert new data without inserting unrelated data - Example: Cannot add a new course without assigning a student to it - Causes: Required attributes for one entity cannot exist without another entity DELETION ANOMALY: - Problem: Deleting data causes unintended loss of other information - Example: Deleting the only student in a course deletes the course information too - Result: Lose valid data that should be preserved All three are caused by redundancy and poor database design.
questions.e: These anomalies motivate the need for normalization to eliminate redundancy.

questions.q: Given the relation: EMP_PROJ(EmployeeID, EmployeeName, ProjectID, ProjectName, Hours) With FD: EmployeeID → EmployeeName and ProjectID → ProjectName Identify: (a) What normal form is this in? (b) What anomalies exist? (c) How would you decompose it to 3NF?
questions.m: (a) NORMAL FORM: 2NF (or possibly 1NF depending on implementation) - Has partial dependencies: EmployeeID → EmployeeName and ProjectID → ProjectName - Violates 2NF because non-key attributes depend on only part of the composite key (b) ANOMALIES: Update: Changing an employee's name requires updating all their project records Insertion: Cannot add a new employee without assigning them to a project Deletion: Deleting an employee's last project deletes the employee record (c) DECOMPOSITION TO 3NF: Relation 1: EMPLOYEE(EmployeeID, EmployeeName) Relation 2: PROJECT(ProjectID, ProjectName) Relation 3: EMP_PROJ(EmployeeID, ProjectID, Hours) Functional Dependencies preserved: - EMPLOYEE: EmployeeID → EmployeeName - PROJECT: ProjectID → ProjectName - EMP_PROJ: (EmployeeID, ProjectID) → Hours Result: All relations in 3NF, anomalies eliminated
questions.e: Decomposition separates independent entities and their relationships.

questions.q: Consider: STUDENT_COURSE(StudentID, StudentName, Major, CourseID, CourseName, Grade) With FD: StudentID → StudentName, StudentID → Major, CourseID → CourseName Identify: (a) Current normal form, (b) All dependencies, (c) Decompose to 3NF.
questions.m: (a) NORMAL FORM: 1NF or violates 2NF - Partial dependencies exist - Multiple non-key attributes depend on only parts of the composite key (b) ALL FUNCTIONAL DEPENDENCIES: - StudentID → StudentName (partial dependency) - StudentID → Major (partial dependency) - CourseID → CourseName (partial dependency) - (StudentID, CourseID) → Grade (full dependency) (c) DECOMPOSITION TO 3NF: Relation 1: STUDENT(StudentID, StudentName, Major) Relation 2: COURSE(CourseID, CourseName) Relation 3: ENROLLMENT(StudentID, CourseID, Grade) Verification: - STUDENT: StudentID is primary key, all non-key attributes depend on it - COURSE: CourseID is primary key, all non-key attributes depend on it - ENROLLMENT: (StudentID, CourseID) is primary key, Grade depends on it - All in 3NF, no anomalies
questions.e: Separate entities (Student, Course) from their relationship (Enrollment).

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a key attribute?
o: An attribute that is frequently accessed
An attribute that uniquely identifies a tuple
An attribute that must not be NULL
An attribute that appears in multiple tables
questions.e: A key attribute (or key) is a minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies each tuple in a relation. A prime attribute is any attribute that is part of some candidate key.

questions.q: What is the relationship between a determinant and BCNF?
o: A determinant is another name for a key
BCNF requires that every determinant is a candidate key
questions.e: A determinant is any attribute on which another attribute is functionally dependent. BCNF requires that every determinant must be a candidate key of the relation.

questions.q: Which component of DBMS architecture is responsible for converting logical plans into physical execution plans?
questions.e: The optimizer chooses an efficient physical execution plan for a parsed logical query plan.

questions.q: A relation R(A, B, C, D) has functional dependencies A -> B, B -> C, and C -> D. What is a candidate key?
questions.e: A determines B, then C, then D, so A+ = ABCD. No smaller set exists.

questions.q: Horizontal scaling (scaling out) in NoSQL means:
o: Adding more servers to distribute data and load
Adding more CPU/RAM to existing servers
questions.e: Horizontal scaling distributes data and workload across multiple machines.

questions.q: NoSQL databases are commonly used because they:
o: Do not support any data model
Support flexibility in schema and distributed scalability
questions.e: A major NoSQL motivation is flexible schema design and distributed scale.

questions.q: Given R(A, B) = {(1,2), (3,4)} and S(B, C) = {(2,5), (6,7)}, what is R natural join S?
questions.e: Only B = 2 appears in both relations, producing tuple (A=1, B=2, C=5).

questions.q: Relational algebra is:
o: The original theoretical foundation for SQL
questions.e: Relational algebra is the formal query model that underlies relational query languages.

questions.q: A database system enforces atomicity and durability but not consistency and isolation. Which scenario is possible?
o: Two transactions see each other's uncommitted changes, leading to dirty reads
A transaction is partially committed after a system crash
The database violates a foreign key constraint after a successful transaction
questions.e: Missing isolation permits dirty reads; missing consistency could also permit constraint violations. Atomicity makes option B false, so D is false.

questions.q: In a three-tier database architecture, where does business logic primarily reside?
questions.e: The middle/application tier normally contains business rules and application logic.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a property of a good decomposition in normalization?
questions.e: Good decomposition aims for lossless join, dependency preservation when possible, and reduced redundancy, not simply more tables.

questions.q: Denormalization is typically done to:
o: Improve query performance at the cost of redundancy
questions.e: Denormalization deliberately reintroduces redundancy to reduce joins or speed up read-heavy workloads.

questions.q: Which scenario is best suited for a document database like MongoDB?
o: Banking transactions requiring strict ACID guarantees
Content management systems with flexible schemas
Real-time bidirectional relationships such as social networks
questions.e: Document databases fit semi-structured content with flexible document shapes.

questions.q: An OODBMS is most suitable for applications requiring:
questions.e: Object-oriented DBMSs are useful when data is naturally represented as complex objects with identity and behavior.

questions.q: The User entity has a multivalued composite attribute Interests with sub-attributes music and movies. Which mapping strategy is most normalized and flexible for adding new interests?
o: User_Interests(UserId, interest_type, interest_value) with PK(UserId, interest_type, interest_value)
Interests(interest_id, interest_type, interest_value) and User_Interests(UserId, interest_id)
questions.e: A separate Interests lookup plus associative table avoids repeating interest values and supports new interest types flexibly.

questions.q: Blog_Posting is a weak entity identified through User -> Blog and Blog -> Blog_Posting. Which schema correctly maps Blog_Posting?
o: Blog_Posting(URL, timestamp, msg) with PK(URL, timestamp) and FK(URL) references Blog(URL)
Blog_Posting(UserId, URL, timestamp, msg) with PK(UserId, URL, timestamp) and FK(UserId, URL) references Blog(UserId, URL)
Blog_Posting(PostingId, URL, timestamp, msg) with surrogate PK(PostingId)
questions.e: A weak entity key includes the owner key plus its partial key. Under the stated chain, Blog is identified by UserId and URL, so Blog_Posting uses UserId, URL, timestamp.

questions.q: Which relational schema maps Friendship and enforces that a user cannot be friends with themselves?
o: Friendship(sender_id, recipient_id, status), PK(sender_id, recipient_id), two FKs to User
Friendship(friendship_id, sender_id, recipient_id, status), PK(friendship_id), two FKs to User, CHECK(sender_id <> recipient_id)
Friendship(sender_id, recipient_id, status), PK(sender_id, recipient_id), two FKs to User, CHECK(sender_id <= recipient_id)
Friendship(sender_id, recipient_id, status), PK(sender_id), two FKs to User, CHECK(sender_id <> recipient_id)
questions.e: The self-friend rule requires CHECK(sender_id <> recipient_id). A production design should also add UNIQUE(sender_id, recipient_id) if duplicate pairs are not allowed.

questions.q: Announce connects User (1) to Event (N). Event has total participation and User has partial participation. Which implementation is most appropriate?
o: Put NOT NULL announcer_id in Event as FK to User(UserId)
questions.e: For a 1:N relationship, place the FK on the N side. Total participation of Event means the FK is NOT NULL.

questions.q: Has between User and Blog is 1:1. Blog participation is total, User participation is partial, and Blog has dependent weak entities. Which mapping is optimal?
o: Merge User and Blog, making Blog attributes nullable
Place UserId as NOT NULL FK in Blog; do not merge because Blog has dependent weak entities
Place URL as nullable FK in User
Create Has(UserId, URL) as separate table
questions.e: For 1:1 with total participation on Blog, a NOT NULL FK in Blog works well. Keeping Blog separate preserves its dependent weak entities.

questions.q: BORROW has composite PK {ItemID, BorrowerID, RequestDate}. What does including RequestDate indicate?
o: BORROW is a weak entity identified by ITEM and SWAPPER
The same swapper can borrow the same item multiple times on different dates
RequestDate is a partial key of a weak entity BORROW
There is a ternary relationship among ITEM, SWAPPER, and DATE
questions.e: If ItemID and BorrowerID alone are not enough, RequestDate distinguishes repeated borrow requests for the same item and borrower.

questions.q: BORROW has ReturnCondition as a nullable FK referencing CONDITION. In the ER model, this best represents:
o: Total participation of BORROW with CONDITION
Partial participation of BORROW in a relationship with CONDITION
CONDITION is a weak entity dependent on BORROW
questions.e: A nullable foreign key means a BORROW tuple may exist without a related CONDITION tuple.

questions.q: ITEM has OwnerID referencing SWAPPER, and BORROW has BorrowerID referencing SWAPPER. In ER terms, this represents:
o: Two distinct binary relationships between SWAPPER and ITEM
SWAPPER participating in two different roles: owner and borrower
questions.e: The same entity type SWAPPER plays different roles: owner through ITEM.OwnerID and borrower through BORROW.BorrowerID.

questions.q: GROUP_MEMBERSHIP between SWAPPER and SWAPPER_GROUP has cardinality:
o: M:N because both foreign keys form the composite primary key
Cannot be determined without instance data
questions.e: A bridge table whose primary key is the pair of foreign keys maps a many-to-many relationship.

questions.q: ITEM.OwnerID is a NOT NULL FK to SWAPPER. This maps to which ER concept?
o: Total participation of ITEM in the OWNS relationship
Partial participation of SWAPPER in OWNS
questions.e: Every item must reference an owner, so ITEM participates totally in OWNS.

questions.q: A student claims BORROW should be ternary because it references ITEM, SWAPPER, and CONDITION. This interpretation is:
o: Correct, because BORROW connects three entities simultaneously
Incorrect, because CONDITION is optional and represents return status, not a core participant
Correct, because all three FKs identify a borrow instance
Incorrect, because ternary relationships cannot have nullable participants
questions.e: The identifying participants are item and borrower plus request date. ReturnCondition is optional status information after return, not a core participant.

questions.q: To create table BOOK with Book_id primary key and Publisher_name referencing PUBLISHER(Name), which statement is correct?
o: PRIMARY KEY Book_id and FOREIGN KEY Publisher_name REFERENCES PUBLISHER(Name)
CREATE TABLE BOOK (Book_id INT PRIMARY KEY, Title VARCHAR(100), Publisher_name VARCHAR(50), FOREIGN KEY (Publisher_name) REFERENCES PUBLISHER(Name));
Publisher_name VARCHAR(50) FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES PUBLISHER(Name), PRIMARY KEY(Book_id)
questions.e: The FK column is declared, and the table-level foreign key references PUBLISHER(Name) with correct parentheses.

questions.q: Which statement removes the foreign key constraint named fk_publisher from BOOK?
o: ALTER TABLE BOOK DROP FOREIGN KEY fk_publisher;
ALTER TABLE BOOK REMOVE CONSTRAINT fk_publisher;
ALTER TABLE BOOK DELETE FOREIGN KEY fk_publisher;
questions.e: In MySQL-style syntax, DROP FOREIGN KEY constraint_name removes a foreign key constraint.

questions.q: Rename column Address to Location in LIBRARY_BRANCH.
o: ALTER TABLE LIBRARY_BRANCH RENAME Address TO Location;
ALTER TABLE LIBRARY_BRANCH CHANGE COLUMN Address Location VARCHAR;
ALTER TABLE LIBRARY_BRANCH RENAME COLUMN Address TO Location;
ALTER TABLE LIBRARY_BRANCH ALTER Address RENAME Location;
questions.e: Standard syntax is ALTER TABLE table RENAME COLUMN old_name TO new_name.

questions.q: Create a view AVAILABLE_BOOKS showing books whose total copies across branches is greater than zero.
o: CREATE VIEW AVAILABLE_BOOKS AS SELECT B.Book_id, B.Title, SUM(BC.No_of_copies) AS Total FROM BOOK B JOIN BOOK_COPIES BC ON B.Book_id = BC.Book_id GROUP BY B.Book_id, B.Title HAVING SUM(BC.No_of_copies) > 0;
CREATE AVAILABLE_BOOKS VIEW AS ... HAVING Total > 0;
VIEW AVAILABLE_BOOKS CREATE AS ... WHERE SUM(...) > 0;
questions.e: Views use CREATE VIEW name AS SELECT. Aggregate filters belong in HAVING, not WHERE.

questions.q: Which statement changes BORROWER.Phone from VARCHAR(15) to VARCHAR(20)?
o: ALTER TABLE BORROWER CHANGE Phone VARCHAR(20);
ALTER TABLE BORROWER MODIFY Phone VARCHAR(20);
ALTER TABLE BORROWER ALTER COLUMN Phone VARCHAR(20);
ALTER TABLE BORROWER UPDATE COLUMN Phone TYPE VARCHAR(20);
questions.e: In MySQL-style syntax, MODIFY changes a column definition while keeping the name.

questions.q: Create LIBRARY_BRANCH where Branch_name cannot be NULL or the empty string.
o: Branch_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL NO EMPTY
Both B and C are correct
questions.e: NOT NULL prevents missing names and CHECK prevents empty strings. Option C still allows NULL in many SQL systems because CHECK evaluates UNKNOWN.

questions.q: Find borrowers who have never borrowed any book.
questions.m: SELECT b.* FROM BORROWER b WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM BOOK_LOANS l WHERE l.Card_no = b.Card_no );

questions.q: Find the publisher(s) that published the maximum number of books.
questions.m: SELECT Publisher_name FROM BOOK GROUP BY Publisher_name HAVING COUNT(*) >= ALL ( SELECT COUNT(*) FROM BOOK GROUP BY Publisher_name );

questions.q: Find pairs of borrowers who have borrowed the same book. Return each pair only once.
questions.m: SELECT DISTINCT l1.Card_no AS borrower1, l2.Card_no AS borrower2, l1.Book_id FROM BOOK_LOANS l1 JOIN BOOK_LOANS l2 ON l1.Book_id = l2.Book_id AND l1.Card_no < l2.Card_no;

questions.q: Find books along with the total copies across all branches.
questions.m: SELECT b.Book_id, b.Title, SUM(bc.No_of_copies) AS total_copies FROM BOOK b JOIN BOOK_COPIES bc ON b.Book_id = bc.Book_id GROUP BY b.Book_id, b.Title;

questions.q: Complete the query to find book-branch combinations with copies exceeding the average.
questions.m: SELECT Book_id, Branch_id, No_of_copies FROM BOOK_COPIES WHERE No_of_copies > ( SELECT AVG(No_of_copies) FROM BOOK_COPIES ) ORDER BY No_of_copies DESC;

questions.q: Paper has relationships with Author (n:1) and Periodical (n:1). What can we infer about a Paper?
o: A Paper can exist without any Author or Periodical
A Paper has association with many Authors and exactly one Periodical
A Paper can have only one Author
A Paper can appear in multiple Periodicals
questions.e: Reading the shown cardinalities, a paper can be associated with many authors and one periodical.

questions.q: Tag has n:n relationships with both Book and Periodical. Which statement best describes Tag?
o: Tag is a weak entity dependent on Book and Periodical
Tag is a categorization/classification mechanism shared across publication types
Each Tag belongs to exactly one Book or Periodical
Tag should be a relationship attribute, not an entity
questions.e: A shared Tag entity supports many-to-many classification of both books and periodicals.

questions.q: Why might the designer use two separate Borrow relationships instead of a generalized BorrowableItem superclass?
o: To allow different attributes/constraints for borrowing different item types
Because ER diagrams cannot represent generalization of relationships
This is always a modeling flaw
questions.e: Separate relationships can represent different rules, attributes, or constraints for books and periodicals.

questions.q: Author has only Id and Name. To track an author affiliation, what ER modification is needed?
o: Add affiliation as an attribute to Author
Add affiliation to the Has relationship
questions.e: If each author has one simple affiliation value, an Author attribute is enough. A separate entity is only needed for richer or multiple affiliations.

questions.q: If a new Paper is added, based on the shown cardinalities, which associations are mandatory?
o: Both Author and Periodical associations are mandatory
questions.e: The diagram and question wording imply Paper must be connected to both its author side and its containing periodical.

questions.q: Borrow between User and Book is n:n. To ensure a User cannot borrow the same Book twice simultaneously, what does this imply?
o: Add a constraint not fully expressed in basic ER notation
questions.e: This is a temporal/business rule, usually enforced by a key or assertion over active loans rather than simple cardinality alone.

questions.q: Design an EER hierarchy that removes redundancy by creating Publication, adds Thesis, allows overlap, requires every publication to be in at least one subclass, and moves shared relationships upward.
questions.m: Create superclass Publication with common attributes such as PublicationId, Title, Year, and possibly ISBN/identifier when shared. Make Book, Periodical, and Thesis subclasses. Thesis has Degree, University, Advisor, and DefenseDate. The specialization is total and overlapping: every Publication must be at least one subtype, and a Publication may belong to more than one subtype if the domain allows it. Move relationships shared by Book and Periodical, such as Borrow by User, Has Tag, and Has Publisher, to Publication. Keep subtype-specific relationships such as Periodical containing Paper at the Periodical level.

questions.q: Allow users to borrow both Publications and Equipment through a unified borrowing system. Equipment and Publication share no common attributes, but share borrowable behavior. Not all items must be borrowable.
questions.m: Use a category/union type or shared role entity named BorrowableItem whose superclasses are Publication and Equipment. Equipment has EquipmentId, Name, SerialNumber, PurchaseDate, and Condition. Because not all Publications or Equipment are borrowable, membership in BorrowableItem is partial. Relate User to BorrowableItem through Borrow, with attributes BorrowDate, DueDate, ItemType, and ItemName. ItemType can identify whether the borrowed item came from Publication or Equipment; ItemName may be derived from the source item.

questions.q: Authors can be Individual Authors or Organizational Authors. Some Individual Authors are also Users. Model this using EER constructs.
questions.m: Model Author as a category or superclass with two disjoint subtypes: IndividualAuthor and OrganizationalAuthor. IndividualAuthor has PId, BirthDate, Nationality, and ORCID. OrganizationalAuthor has Id, FoundedYear, Headquarters, and Type. Since some IndividualAuthors are also Users, create an overlapping relationship/category between IndividualAuthor and User, or model Person as a shared superclass with User and IndividualAuthor as overlapping roles/subclasses.

questions.q: For R(CustomerID, CustomerName, SaleID, SaleDate, ProductID, ProductName, RegionID, RegionName), which is a valid candidate key?
questions.e: CustomerID gives CustomerName; SaleID gives ProductID; ProductID gives ProductName; the pair CustomerID, SaleID gives SaleDate and RegionID, and RegionID gives RegionName.

questions.q: Show that there is or is not a second candidate key.
questions.m: There is no second candidate key from the given FDs. SaleID alone determines ProductID and ProductName, but not CustomerID, CustomerName, SaleDate, RegionID, or RegionName. CustomerID alone determines only CustomerName. ProductID and RegionID determine only their descriptive names. The only minimal set that determines all attributes is (CustomerID, SaleID).

questions.q: Decompose R to BCNF and show the main steps.
questions.m: One BCNF decomposition is: R1(CustomerID, CustomerName) for CustomerID -> CustomerName R2(ProductID, ProductName) for ProductID -> ProductName R3(RegionID, RegionName) for RegionID -> RegionName R4(SaleID, ProductID) for SaleID -> ProductID R5(CustomerID, SaleID, SaleDate, RegionID) where (CustomerID, SaleID) is the key. Each determinant in these relations is a key, so the result is in BCNF.

questions.q: Which of the following is part of the BCNF final decomposition?
questions.e: Strictly applying FD5 means A still violates BCNF because SaleID -> ProductID and SaleID is not a superkey. So none of the listed options is fully correct; A is the closest expected exam choice before splitting SaleID -> ProductID.

questions.q: Which option exhibits an insert anomaly?
questions.e: Because RegionName depends on RegionID, storing it only with CustomerID makes it hard to insert a new region unless a customer row exists.

questions.q: Which query returns all orders where status is shipped?
questions.e: status is a top-level scalar field, so match it directly.

questions.q: Which query returns all orders that do not contain any item with product Mouse?
questions.e: Using dot notation on items.product with $nin excludes documents where the array contains Mouse. {$not: {$elemMatch: {product:"Mouse"}}} is another robust form.

questions.q: Which query selects orders that are shipped and made by a VIP customer?
questions.e: status is top-level, and customer.vip is a nested field addressed with dot notation.

questions.q: Which aggregation pipeline returns total revenue per product, sorted highest to lowest?
o: Group by $items.product and sum $items.price, then sort
Group by $items.product and sum $multiply of qty and price, then sort
Project product and revenue, then sort
Unwind items, use $sum as a stage, then sort
questions.e: The correct idea is group revenue by product using qty * price, but a fully correct MongoDB pipeline must first unwind items, then group and sort.

questions.q: Choose the steps for designing and implementing a database in the correct order: Create your own application Decide how to query Logical modeling Conceptual modeling Optimize the design
questions.e: ✓ Correct Answer: B The proper database design sequence is: Conceptual modeling (ER diagrams) → Logical modeling (relational schema) → Optimize (normalization) → Query design (SQL) → Application development. Why this order? Database design follows a top-down approach, starting from abstract concepts and moving to concrete implementation.

questions.q: Storing the same data in many places is called:
questions.e: ✓ Correct Answer: B - Redundancy Redundancy leads to data inconsistency and wastes storage.

questions.q: Which enables users to modify data structures without affecting existing programs?
questions.e: ✓ Correct Answer: A - Data Independence Allows schema changes at one level without affecting higher levels.

questions.q: What is TRUE about the Conceptual level?
o: Describes what data is stored and relationships
questions.e: ✓ Correct Answer: D - All of the above The conceptual level provides a complete abstract view of the database.

questions.q: Which architecture is common for web applications?
questions.e: ✓ Correct Answer: C - Three tiers Presentation → Business Logic → Data layers.

questions.q: Which ACID property ensures committed changes persist despite failures?
questions.e: ✓ Correct Answer: D - Durability Ensures permanent storage of committed transactions.

questions.q: Which offers the ability to query and manipulate data?
questions.e: ✓ Correct Answer: D - DML SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE are DML commands.

questions.q: If every non-key attribute is functionally dependent on the primary key, the relation is in:
questions.e: ✓ Correct Answer: B - Third Normal Form 3NF eliminates transitive dependencies.

questions.q: Explain First Normal Form (1NF) and describe violations that prevent a relation from being in 1NF.
questions.m: ✓ Model Answer A relation is in 1NF if all attributes contain only atomic (indivisible) values. Violations: Multivalued attributes, composite attributes, repeating groups, nested relations.

questions.q: Explain Second Normal Form (2NF) and the type of functional dependency that must be eliminated.
questions.m: ✓ Model Answer A relation is in 2NF if it's in 1NF and every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on the entire primary key. Must eliminate: Partial dependencies (non-prime attributes depending on part of a composite key).

questions.q: Explain Third Normal Form (3NF) and what must be eliminated to achieve it.
questions.m: ✓ Model Answer A relation is in 3NF if it's in 2NF and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on the primary key. Must eliminate: Transitive dependencies (A → B → C where B is non-prime).

questions.q:
Write a SQL query to find customers who have placed orders totaling more than $500.
Schema: Customers (CustomerID, Name), Orders (OrderID, CustomerID, TotalAmount)
questions.m: ✓ Model Answer SELECT C.Name, SUM(O.TotalAmount) AS Total FROM Customers C JOIN Orders O ON C.CustomerID = O.CustomerID GROUP BY C.CustomerID, C.Name HAVING SUM(O.TotalAmount) > 500;

questions.q:
Write SQL queries to:
1. List all unique cities where customers live
2. Insert a new customer
3. Update a customer's address
questions.m: ✓ Model Answer -- 1. Unique cities SELECT DISTINCT City FROM Customers; -- 2. Insert customer INSERT INTO Customers (CustomerID, Name, City) VALUES (101, 'John Doe', 'Riyadh'); -- 3. Update address UPDATE Customers SET Address = '123 Main St' WHERE CustomerID = 101;

questions.q:
Normalize the LIBRARY relation to 3NF:

LIBRARY (Branch#, Branch_Addr, ISBN, Title, Author, Pub_ID, Pub_Name, Pub_Address, Num_copies)

FD1: Branch# → Branch_Addr
FD2: ISBN → Title, Author, Pub_ID
FD3: Pub_ID → Pub_Name, Pub_Address
FD4: (ISBN, Branch#) → Num_copies

Show all steps and final relations.
questions.m: ✓ Model Answer 2NF Decomposition (eliminate partial dependencies): BRANCH (Branch#, Branch_Addr) BOOK (ISBN, Title, Author, Pub_ID, Pub_Name, Pub_Address) INVENTORY (ISBN, Branch#, Num_copies) 3NF Decomposition (eliminate transitive dependencies): BRANCH (Branch#, Branch_Addr) PUBLISHER (Pub_ID, Pub_Name, Pub_Address) BOOK (ISBN, Title, Author, Pub_ID) FK: Pub_ID INVENTORY (ISBN, Branch#, Num_copies) FK: ISBN, Branch#
